problem: Open-vocabulary 3D representations built from foundation-model features store a dense per-point (or implicit) feature vector. This makes them memory-heavy, hard to scale to large scenes, and hard to decompose or update. They also lack explicit inter-object relations, which planners need. Existing 3D scene graphs are compact and structured but closed-vocabulary.
motivation: Robots need a scene representation built online that stays scalable, is open-vocabulary, and offers a flexible level of detail: dense geometry for mobility and manipulation, abstract semantics and affordances for task planning. 2D foundation models (SAM, CLIP, LLaVA, GPT-4) already give strong open-vocabulary semantics. Fusing their object-level outputs into a 3D graph, instead of per-pixel features, gives compactness and structure. It also yields a text form that an LLM can reason over.
key_idea: Fuse class-agnostic 2D instance masks and their CLIP features across posed RGB-D views into 3D object nodes. Caption each node with LLaVA+GPT-4, infer edges with GPT-4 over an MST of 3D-box overlaps, and serialize the resulting open-vocabulary 3D scene graph to JSON for LLM-based task planning.
insight: Object-level fusion, rather than per-point features, keeps the map compact while matching or beating dense feature fusion on open-vocabulary segmentation. On Replica, mAcc is 40.63 vs 24.16 for ConceptFusion and 31.53 for ConceptFusion+SAM, though F-mIoU of 35.95 is below ConceptFusion+SAM's 38.70. The retrieval comparison is the most instructive result. CLIP-embedding retrieval does well on descriptive queries but fails on affordance and negation queries. An LLM reading the node captions handles these much better: Replica negation R@1 is 0.80 vs 0.26 for CLIP, and REAL Lab negation R@1 is 1.00 vs 0.00. So the text-serialized scene graph is what enables compositional reasoning. The bottleneck is caption quality: node precision is about 0.71, and errors are attributed mainly to LLaVA, e.g. small objects labeled as toothbrushes or scissors. Greedy association was found almost as good as Hungarian matching and faster.
method: Class-agnostic 2D segmentation: SAM masks per RGB frame (variant CG-D instead uses the RAM tagger + Grounding DINO boxes). Each mask is encoded with CLIP, back-projected with depth and pose, DBSCAN-denoised, and moved to the map frame.

Object association: for each new detection vs overlapping map objects, similarity = semantic (normalized CLIP cosine, f^T f/2+1/2) + geometric (fraction of points with a nearest neighbor within δ_nn=2.5cm). Greedy matching; a new object is created if similarity < δ_sim=1.1.

Object fusion: running-mean update of the CLIP feature over the number of detections; point-cloud union followed by 2.5cm voxel downsampling. CG-D merges background classes (wall/floor/ceiling) regardless of similarity.

Node captioning: up to the 10 best views per object (ranked by noise-free points contributed) are captioned by LLaVA-7B ('describe the central object in the image'). GPT-4 summarizes these into an object_tag and caption, or marks the node invalid.

Edge generation: pairwise 3D bounding-box IoU gives a dense graph, pruned by a minimum spanning tree. For each MST edge, GPT-4 receives both captions and 3D locations and outputs an open-vocabulary relation (e.g. 'a on b', 'may be stored in') with an explanation.

LLM planner interface: each node is serialized to JSON (id, bbox extent/center, tag, caption) and given to GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613, 8K context). GPT-4 returns ranked relevant object ids. The selected object's 3D pose goes to downstream navigation (ROS costmap on a Jackal) or grasping (Spot Arm) pipelines.

Downstream extensions: LLaVA checks whether the target is visible, with GPT-4 re-querying for likely containers (object search). GPT-4 traversability classification feeds non-traversable objects into the costmap. A particle-filter 3-DoF localization and map update in AI2-THOR matches detections to map objects.

setting.backbone: SAM + CLIP image encoder (frozen) for mapping; LLaVA-7B (frozen) for view captions; GPT-4 gpt-4-0613 (frozen API) for caption summarization, edge relations and query planning. CG-D variant adds RAM + Grounding DINO.
setting.observation: posed RGB-D image sequence (Replica sequences; real scans with Azure Kinect + RTAB-Map poses); onboard RGB-D/RealSense camera + VLP-16 LiDAR on robots
setting.action_space: object-level goal selection (3D pose/bbox of the chosen object) passed to a standard ROS navigation costmap planner or grasping pipeline
setting.simulator: Replica (offline RGB-D sequences), AI2-THOR/ProcTHOR (localization demo); real world (Clearpath Jackal, Boston Dynamics Spot Arm)
setting.privileged: The scene is pre-mapped before querying (pre-exploration). Camera poses come from the dataset (Replica) or RTAB-Map, and the real-world scene cloud is registered to the robot's prior LiDAR map.

numbers_note: No standard embodied-navigation benchmark is used. Navigation (Jackal object search, traversability), mobile manipulation (Spot pick-and-place) and AI2-THOR localization/map-update results are qualitative demos only, shown in figures and video. Quantitative results are Replica open-vocab 3D segmentation, AMT-judged scene-graph accuracy and text-query object retrieval. Precision and recall fractions are converted to 0-100. Per-scene node precision, valid-object and duplicate counts are in Table I but not listed here. The text claims about 90% average edge precision, while the table reports 0.88 for CG and 0.91 for CG-D. Lab R@2/R@3 are printed as '--' where R@1 is already 1.00.
results: On Replica open-vocabulary 3D segmentation, ConceptGraphs reaches 40.63 mAcc / 35.95 F-mIoU. This beats ConceptFusion (24.16/31.31) and ConceptFusion+SAM on mAcc (31.53), but trails the latter on F-mIoU (38.70), at a much smaller memory footprint. Human-evaluated scene graphs reach about 0.71 node and 0.88 edge precision for CG (CG-D: 0.61 and 0.91), with 0-5 duplicates per scene. LLM retrieval over the graph far outperforms CLIP retrieval on affordance and negation queries: Replica negation R@1 is 0.80 vs 0.26, and Lab affordance/negation R@1 is 1.00 vs 0.40/0.00. It also enables real-robot object search and traversability-aware navigation.
limitations: Node captions are error-prone because of LLaVA-7B (about 70% node precision; small objects often mislabeled as toothbrushes or scissors). Small or thin objects are missed and duplicate detections occur, which can break downstream plans.

The map is built offline from a pre-scanned posed RGB-D sequence; captioning and edges run after the whole sequence is processed. Navigation relies on standard costmap planners and is shown only in qualitative demos.
Many LLaVA calls plus proprietary GPT-4 calls add compute and monetary cost. Large scenes can exceed the LLM context length (the authors defer to SayPlan-style hierarchical planning).
